entities.summary:
Ghana, officially the Republic of Ghana, is a country in West Africa bordered by the Gulf of Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso, and Togo. With 34 million people, Ghana is one of West Africa's most stable democracies and a model for African democratic governance since its return to civilian rule in 1993. It is not geographically related to the ancient Empire of Ghana (7th–13th centuries CE), which was located further north and west.

Ghana's territory was home to the Ashanti Empire (1701–1900), one of West Africa's most powerful and sophisticated pre-colonial states — whose gold wealth, intricate kente cloth traditions, and military organization made it a formidable force that resisted British colonization for over a century (four Anglo-Ashanti Wars, 1823–1901). British Gold Coast colony (1874–1957) exploited cocoa and gold while educating an African elite that would lead independence. Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana to independence on March 6, 1957 — the first Black African country south of the Sahara to achieve independence — declaring 'Ghana, your beloved country, is free forever.'

Nkrumah's pan-African vision (founding of the Organisation of African Unity, 1963) made Ghana the symbolic center of African liberation. Military coups (1966, 1972, 1979, 1981) disrupted democratic governance until the 1992 constitution and 1993 elections. Ghana has since undergone seven peaceful democratic transfers of power — exceptional in the African context — while maintaining one of Africa's most open economies, sustained by gold, cocoa, and oil exports.
